clue.text: Sit and canoodle, forming bond together

indicators.note: forming suggests the letters of the two words are shaped into something new

explanation.surface: Two people sit together kissing and cuddling, and their relationship grows stronger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'canoodle' is British slang for kissing and cuddling; the surface romance hides that 'forming' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To consolidate is to combine or strengthen things into a single firm whole, a synonym of bonding.

clue.text: A willing rider

parts.note: read 'willing' as 'relating to a will': a rider added to a will, not a keen horseman

explanation.surface: Someone eager to get on a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'willing' looks like eager, but here it means belonging to a will, and a rider is an added clause.
explanation.definitionFit: A codicil is a supplement that amends or adds to an existing will, i.e. a legal rider to it.

clue.text: Panic, heading round concealed corner

indicators.note: concealed tells us the letters sit unseen within the words that come before it

explanation.surface: A panicking runner heads round a corner to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'Panic' and the start of 'heading'; 'round' simply links.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a recess or nook, a small corner set into a wall or space.

clue.text: It's not even considered mathematically

parts.note: 'not even' sounds like 'not even considered' (ignored), but in arithmetic it describes a value that cannot be halved into whole numbers

explanation.surface: Something dismissed as unworthy of mathematical attention.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the phrase as 'not even', considered mathematically, rather than 'not even considered'.
explanation.definitionFit: Integers like 3 or 7 are not divisible by two; mathematicians call them odd rather than even.

clue.text: I'd look up to this hero

parts.note: the clue's I'd taken as written without the apostrophe

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone the speaker would admire as a hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look up to' reads as admire, which also suits the definition, but 'up' is the reversal signal working on the old word for 'look'.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol is a person greatly admired or worshipped, much as a hero is.

clue.text: He'll kill animals in the end

indicators.note: the end says this last piece is placed after the others, finishing the word

parts.note: an ass is a donkey; the plural word supplies two of them
the second of the two donkeys the plural supplies
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that a hunter will kill the animals in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'animals' gives two asses, ASS twice, and 'in the end' puts IN last.
explanation.definitionFit: An assassin is a murderer, someone who will kill a chosen target.

clue.text: No longer lie about being an outcast

parts.note: ex- describes something former, no longer current

indicators.note: about here means round and about, so the three letters of lie are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone resolving to stop telling untruths about being shunned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' is the prefix meaning former; 'about' is the anagram signal, and 'being' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: An exile is a person banished from their homeland, an outcast from it.

clue.text: Deceives daughter and flees

parts.note: eludes means escapes or flees from

explanation.surface: A daughter tricks her parents and runs away.
explanation.definitionFit: To delude someone is to mislead or trick them into a false belief.

clue.text: Go off, taking girlfriend around school

indicators.note: around says the partner's word wraps about the school's name

parts.note: a date is a romantic partner one goes out with
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Losing one's temper while showing a girlfriend round a school.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton College is the famous English boarding school near Windsor; 'around' is the container signal and 'taking' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: To detonate is to explode, which is what a bomb does when it goes off.

clue.text: Such trees are barely recognisable in winter

definitions.text: Such trees are barely recognisable in winter

parts.words: Such trees are barely recognisable in winter
parts.note: barely suggests hardly, but the trees are literally bare, having shed their leaves

explanation.surface: Trees that are hard to identify in the cold season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barely' means stripped bare as well as hardly.
explanation.definitionFit: Deciduous trees shed their leaves each autumn, leaving them leafless through the winter months.

clue.text: Indeed, all the odd bits will be perfect

indicators.note: the odd bits are the first, third, fifth letters and so on of the words named

explanation.surface: An emphatic claim that all the strange pieces will turn out flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' looks like strange, but it picks positions one, three, five, seven and nine.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal example is a flawless one, so the adjective is a synonym of perfect.

clue.text: High-spirited child?

parts.note: high-spirited looks like lively, but read it as a spirit living on high, in heaven

explanation.surface: A lively, boisterous youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: Taken literally, a spirit up high in the shape of a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is a winged angel usually pictured as a chubby infant, a heavenly spirit in child form.

clue.text: A fashion editor's heavenly body

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the letters of editor's are reshaped

explanation.surface: A fashion editor with a stunning figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' looks like a noun describing the editor, but it is a verb shuffling EDITORS into STEROID.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a small rocky object orbiting the sun, one of the bodies of the heavens.

clue.text: Deposit covers new bid that's reserved

indicators.note: covers says the depositing word wraps round the remaining letters

parts.note: to lay something is to deposit or set it down

indicators.note: new suggests bid is remade into a fresh order of its letters

explanation.surface: A bank deposit underwrites a fresh offer that has been held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deposit' looks like a noun about money but is the verb meaning set down; 'new' is the anagram signal and 'covers' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Something laid by has been put aside or saved for later, kept in reserve.

clue.text: Dissect an insect, for example

indicators.note: to dissect is to cut apart, so the letters of the words that follow are taken to pieces and rebuilt

explanation.surface: A biology lesson suggesting a bug to cut up as a specimen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' links, and 'for instance' equals 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a case or illustration of something, a synonym of an example.

clue.text: I was told off for youthful indiscretions

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so the letters of the words before it are out of order

explanation.surface: Someone recalling being scolded for the reckless things done when young.
explanation.walkthrough: 'told off' looks like a scolding; 'off' alone shuffles I WAS TOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: Sowing one's wild oats means indulging in reckless or promiscuous behaviour while young.

clue.text: Respect some hesitation in one's excuses, perhaps …

indicators.note: in places the hesitation sound within the word for excuses

parts.note: a defence is the case one makes for oneself, of which excuses are an example
er is the sound a speaker makes when hesitating

explanation.surface: Showing respect by hesitating a little before offering excuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks excuses as only one kind of case made for oneself; 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Deference is polite submission or regard shown to another, a form of respect.

clue.text: … respect I fancy they will show one's paid

indicators.note: fancy, meaning elaborate or ornamental, tells us the letters before it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a person admits liking respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' looks like a verb meaning like, but it is the anagram signal for RESPECT I.
explanation.definitionFit: Receipts are written acknowledgements given as proof that a payment has been made.

clue.text: Not the same as put into proper order

parts.note: taken as written
sorted means arranged in order

explanation.surface: Something differs from what has been neatly arranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Assorted items are of various kinds, mixed and different from one another.

clue.text: A couple of pages to praise and praise

parts.note: p is the abbreviation for page, and two of them make pp
to laud is to praise highly

explanation.surface: A pair of book pages devoted to lavish commendation.
explanation.definitionFit: To applaud is to clap or express approval, a way of showing praise.

clue.text: Bids for chests without a number

indicators.note: without says the number is taken away from the word for chests

parts.note: coffers are strongboxes or chests for valuables
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Offers made for treasure chests lacking a catalogue number.
explanation.walkthrough: C, Roman numeral 100, leaves COFFERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Offers are proposals of a price, the same as bids at an auction.

clue.text: Country seen differently by upset convict

indicators.note: differently says the letters of seen are put in another order
in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read from the bottom up

parts.note: a lag is slang for a convict, especially an old lag

explanation.surface: A nation viewed in a new light by a disgruntled prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'differently' gives SENE from SEEN; 'upset' turns LAG into GAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Senegal is a nation in West Africa whose capital is Dakar.

clue.text: Theatre attendant

parts.note: attendant looks like a member of staff such as an usher, but here means one who attends a show

explanation.surface: An usher working at a playhouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Not a worker but someone attending the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A playgoer is a person who regularly goes to watch plays, a member of the audience.

clue.text: Attendance down, at first, restricted to college

parts.note: the gate is the number of spectators attending a match

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A football report: the crowd is down initially.
explanation.walkthrough: A GATE is a sports crowd. At British universities, being gated is a punishment that confines a student to college.
explanation.definitionFit: Being gated at Oxford or Cambridge means a student is confined within the college as a punishment.

clue.text: Where most are bent on entering?

definitions.text: Where most are bent on entering?

parts.words: Where most are bent on entering?
parts.note: bent on looks like determined to, but bent is slang for crooked, so the crooked are mostly on entering

explanation.surface: A place nearly everyone is keen to get into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bent' is British slang for corrupt or criminal; read as 'most are bent' when they enter.
explanation.definitionFit: A jail's inmates are criminals, the crooked people locked up there.

clue.text: An account to settle?

parts.note: account suggests a bill to pay, but the phrase is about settling an old grudge

explanation.surface: A bill that needs paying.
explanation.walkthrough: One settles a score as an old grievance; a score was also a tally or bill.
explanation.definitionFit: A score can mean a grievance or a running tally of debts, both things one may settle.

clue.text: Lovely article in wood

indicators.note: in places the article within the tree's name

parts.note: fir is a conifer and its timber
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A beautiful item found in a forest.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair in its old sense means beautiful or attractive, as in a fair maiden.

clue.text: Fashionable racecourse for a northerner

parts.note: a Scot comes from Scotland, the north of Britain

explanation.surface: A smart racecourse suited to someone from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is the Berkshire racecourse known for Royal Ascot and its hats.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is an English racecourse famous for its high-society meeting and showy fashion.

clue.text: Chant a simple ditty

parts.note: plain means simple or unadorned
a ditty is a short simple song

explanation.surface: Singing a modest little tune.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainsong is unaccompanied medieval church music sung in unison, a kind of liturgical chant.

clue.text: Merit good treatment, as hard-working oil-drillers do?

definitions.meaning: to be worthy of being treated well
drillers who serve a well, tending a borehole, do so with diligence

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the phrase as 'serve' plus 'well', the oil well being worked.
explanation.definitionFit: To be worthy of good treatment is to have earned it; oil workers literally tend the well.
